rows.description: Hot, luminous main-sequence stars. Temperate terrestrial planets are possible, but stronger UV and shorter stellar lifetimes make naturally Earthlike worlds less likely.
Hotter and more luminous than the Sun. Temperate terrestrial planets remain plausible despite greater UV exposure.
Sun-like stars and the baseline for long-term temperate terrestrial environments.
Cooler and dimmer than G stars, but stable, long-lived, and highly favorable to habitability.
Red dwarfs. Temperate planets are plausible, but close-in habitable zones have tidal, atmospheric, and stellar-activity complications.
Evolved stars with outward-shifted habitable zones. Existing outer planets or moons can become temperate, though Earthlike worlds are unusual.
Compact stellar remnant. Planets and temporary habitable zones are possible, but naturally Earthlike worlds are exceptional.
Collapsed stellar remnant. Planet formation history and extreme radiation make naturally Earthlike conditions highly improbable.
Collapsed remnant without an ordinary luminous surface. Conventional naturally Earthlike planets require unusual circumstances or another luminous companion.
